key_insight: Interface stability in gas-liquid contactors is governed by opening geometry and wettability, with narrower/elongated openings providing a larger and stiffer pressure window against flooding.
engineering_relevance: For gas diffusion electrodes in organic electrosynthesis, geometry can expand the safe operating window itself, while wettability mainly shifts that window and trades flooding margin against breakthrough margin.
method: Phase-field simulations of the coupled Cahn-Hilliard-Navier-Stokes equations.
Laplace pressure curves used to extract maximum admissible pressure difference and interface stiffness.
Geometry comparison across flat orifices, slits, diamond-shaped openings, and woven meshes.
evidence_signal: The abstract reports that elongating a flat opening from aspect ratio 1 to 6 increases admissible pressure by 40% and stiffness by 3.3×, while wettability in meshes shifts the operating window by several times its stretch.
watch_item: Results are simulation-based and may depend on idealized geometry, surface assumptions, and contact-angle conditions that can be difficult to reproduce in real porous electrodes.
paper_title: Phase-field simulation of interfacial stability in structured gas-liquid contactors: design rules for gas diffusion electrodes
